claims.text: A data-driven model explicitly accounting for approximately 1 wt.% oxygen will predict the thermal conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than analytical defect-free-crystal approximations.
The proposed accuracy advantage will apply in both the near 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The relevant material is HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% incorporated oxygen.
The oxygen-containing alloy retains a typical conventionally cast or thermomechanically processed polycrystalline microstructure.
The model will combine defect-free analytical models, oxygen-specific descriptors, and experimentally derived calibration points.
The computational or artificial-intelligence framework will represent oxygen-induced phonon and electron scattering.
Measurements in both temperature regimes will be made under inert atmosphere or vacuum on the same bulk specimen with consistent geometry and protocols.
Oxygen atoms introduce point defects and localized strain fields in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-induced point defects and strain fields increase phonon scattering relative to a nominally pure, defect-free crystal.
Oxygen-induced point defects and strain fields increase electron scattering relative to a nominally pure, defect-free crystal.
Conventional analytical approaches neglect oxygen-related deformation and electronic-scattering effects.
Explicitly including oxygen-defect scattering channels will improve agreement between predicted and measured thermal conductivity.
The proposed model's deviations from measured conductivity will be approximately 10–20% smaller than those of standard analytical models.
Standard analytical models assume a single-crystalline, defect-free alloy.
Such standard analytical models often underpredict or overpredict actual thermal conduction.
The proposed approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1–2 wt.% oxygen.
The calibrated temperature applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Nonuniform oxygen distributions, microstructural heterogeneity, and approximate dopant-scattering representations may increase prediction error.
Prediction deviations may become larger outside the stated oxygen and temperature limits.
The hypothesis is falsified if the new model has a larger error than the classical model at more than 25% of tested temperature points.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires an approximately 10–20% error reduction, but the falsification rule only rejects the hypothesis when the new model is worse than the baseline at more than 25% of points. A model that provides no 10–20% improvement, or no improvement at all, could therefore fail the stated prediction without meeting the stated falsification criterion.
